title: Five writers share the style catalogue with no exclusion of any kind
body:
## Summary
`pipeline/foundry/styles.json` — the versioned index this module calls "the finding" — is read-modify-written by two app paths and three Python scripts, with no lock, no compare-and-swap and no ownership rule. Two overlapping commits lose one side's styles and answer 200.

## Description
`commitRun` (lib/foundry/store.ts) and `commitExtractRun` (lib/foundry/extract/store.ts) both do `readJson(STYLES)` → mutate in memory → `writeJsonAtomic(STYLES)`, with awaits in between. Nothing serialises them against each other, against a second tab, or against pipeline/foundry/{acquire,forge,intake}.py and pipeline/foundry/extract.mts, which write the same file. `writeJsonAtomic` makes each WRITE atomic and does nothing about the read-modify-write around it — and its temp name is `${file}.${process.pid}.tmp`, so two writers inside ONE process share the temp path and lose even that guarantee. The module already knows this class: `stepRun` keeps an in-process promise chain per run for exactly the same hazard, one file away. Fixed means an exclusion that spans PROCESSES (a lock file with a stale-lock bound, or a read-verify-rewrite), because three of the five writers are not this process — an in-process lock would be the wrong instrument, and the registry's cross-process-exclusion technique names that mistake.

## Flow
- a human commits an extract run in one tab while the forge's intake script writes the catalogue
- both read styles.json; both append; both write
- the later write wins whole-file, and the other side's styles are gone
- both callers were told it worked, and nothing on disk records that anything was lost

## Expected impact
Silent loss of the artefact the whole module exists to produce — the header says the images are only the evidence and these two files ARE the finding. Measured by counting unserialised read-modify-write sequences on the shared path. What could break: a lock file needs a stale bound or a dead writer wedges every future commit, and the Python side has to honour the same protocol or the lock is decorative.

## Evaluation
Claim: resilience — concurrent commits stop losing each other's styles
Before: 5 independent writers of pipeline/foundry/styles.json; 0 locks; 2 of them read-modify-write inside this process sharing one temp filename
After: 5 writers behind 1 cross-process lock with a stale bound; 0 unserialised read-modify-write sequences
Method: probe — enumerated the writers by grep and read the read-modify-write in both app paths
Result: better
Gate: contract
evidence:
lib/foundry/store.ts:278-286 — readJson(STYLES) … await … writeJsonAtomic(STYLES)
lib/foundry/extract/store.ts:309-343 — the same shape
lib/foundry/store.ts:79-84 — writeJsonAtomic's temp is `${file}.${process.pid}.tmp`, shared by two writers in one process
grep -rln 'styles.json' app lib pipeline -> lib/foundry/store.ts, lib/foundry/extract/store.ts, pipeline/foundry/acquire.py, pipeline/foundry/forge.py, pipeline/foundry/intake.py, pipeline/foundry/extract.mts
lib/foundry/extract/store.ts:247 — `locks`, the in-process guard that exists for the per-run case and not for this one

title: Neither commit path is idempotent, so a crash mid-commit double-applies on retry
body:
## Summary
Both commits write the versioned indices BEFORE flipping the run's status to `committed`. A failure in the gap leaves the run re-committable, and the retry appends the same ledger rows and the same style evidence again.

## Description
`commitRun` (lib/foundry/store.ts) performs seven mutations in order: unlink the rejected files, append ledger rows, write LEDGER, append style evidence, write STYLES, write findings.md, write verdicts.json, then set `run.status = "committed"` and write run.json. The `already committed` guard reads that last write, so any failure before it leaves the run open to a second commit — which appends the SAME rows to the append-only ledger and the same evidence to each style. Style promotion reads `keptScenes.size >= 2` over that evidence list, so duplicated evidence can promote a style to `proven` on one human decision counted twice. `commitExtractRun` has the same gap and a sharper symptom: its id minting (`for (let i = 2; taken.has(cid); i++) cid = ...`) turns a re-commit into `style-2` duplicates rather than detecting that the style is already there. Fixed means the append is keyed by run — this run's rows REPLACE this run's rows — so the whole commit is re-entrant wherever it died. A style row also carries `evidence` as a required TS field that nothing validates on read, so a hand-edited catalogue entry without it throws mid-commit, after the ledger has already been written.

## Flow
- a commit writes ledger.json and styles.json, then the process is killed (a deploy, a Cloud Run duration ceiling, a disk error on findings.md)
- run.json still says `done`, so the page offers Commit again
- the retry appends every ledger row a second time and every style evidence entry a second time
- a style with one kept scene now has two evidence rows and is promoted to `proven`

## Expected impact
The permanent, versioned record of what a human decided gets a second copy of itself, and a style can be promoted on evidence that was one decision. Measured by committing, killing after the index write, re-committing, and counting rows. What could break: keying the replace by run id must not touch rows from OTHER runs, and the delete half is genuinely irreversible so it must stay before the indices, not after.

## Evaluation
Claim: resilience — a commit that died halfway can be re-run without doubling what it already wrote
Before: 0 of 2 commit paths are re-entrant; a retry after the index write appends N ledger rows and N evidence entries a second time
After: 2 of 2 re-entrant; a retry writes the same N rows it already wrote
Method: probe — traced the mutation order against the guard that reads its last step, in both paths
Result: better
Gate: contract
evidence:
lib/foundry/store.ts:227-296 — seven mutations; `run.status = "committed"` is the LAST
lib/foundry/store.ts:230 — the guard that reads it
lib/foundry/store.ts:262-275 — `ledger.rows.push(...)` with no key check
lib/foundry/store.ts:279-285 — `s.evidence.push(...)` then `keptScenes.size >= 2` → `proven`
lib/foundry/extract/store.ts:314-342 — the same gap; `taken.has(cid)` mints `style-2` instead of noticing a re-commit
lib/foundry/types.ts:93 — `evidence: Evidence[]` required by the type, unvalidated on read

title: The foundry disk layer cannot be tested without writing to the operator's real catalogue
body:
## Summary
Both store modules resolve their roots from `process.cwd()` as module constants, so the only destructive path in this repository — `commitRun`, which unlinks candidate files — has no probe and cannot get one without mutating the committed pipeline/foundry/styles.json.

## Description
`tests/golden-path/style-extract.probe.spec.ts` drives engine.ts and vocabulary.ts through an IO fake and covers them well. Neither `lib/foundry/store.ts` nor `lib/foundry/extract/store.ts` is imported by any probe, and the reason is structural rather than an omission: `OUT_ROOT`, `FOUNDRY_DIR`, `LEDGER`, `STYLES` and `EXTRACT_ROOT` are module-level constants over `process.cwd()`, and `STYLES` points at a real, committed file holding the operator's nine styles and 87 ledger rows. A probe for `commitRun` would delete real candidate files and append to the real catalogue. So the module holding the repo's only `unlink`, its verdict persistence and its versioned-index writes is verified by nothing, and the two findings above cannot be closed until it is. Fixed means an injection seam — a root passed in, or read from an env var the probes set — which is a structural change across both stores and the pipeline scripts that import them (`pipeline/foundry/extract.mts` destructures the module).

## Flow
- the fix for either finding above is written
- there is nothing to run that would show it worked
- and nothing that would have shown the defect either: both were found by reading, not by a red test

## Expected impact
The destructive path and the versioned-index writer are the two places in this repo where a bug is not recoverable, and they are the two with no coverage. Measured by counting store modules imported by any probe. What could break: an injectable root is a new way to point production at the wrong directory, so the default must stay the cwd constant and the override must be test-only and loud.

## Evaluation
Claim: quality — the destructive path and the index writer become testable, and the two findings above become closable
Before: 0 of 2 store modules covered by any probe; 1 destructive call site with no test; the catalogue a test would have to mutate holds 9 styles and 87 ledger rows
After: 2 of 2 covered against a temp root; the real catalogue untouched
Method: probe — grepped the probe lane for imports of either store and read where the roots are bound
Result: better
Gate: none
evidence:
grep -rn 'lib/foundry/store\|foundry/extract/store' tests/ -> no probe imports either module
lib/foundry/store.ts:37-40 — OUT_ROOT/FOUNDRY_DIR/LEDGER/STYLES from process.cwd()
lib/foundry/extract/store.ts:45-46 — EXTRACT_ROOT/STYLES from process.cwd()
pipeline/foundry/styles.json — 9 real styles; pipeline/foundry/ledger.json — 87 real rows
lib/foundry/store.ts:249 — `await unlink(...)`, the repo's only destructive filesystem call

title: Two extract runs created in the same second with the same slug can take the same id
body:
## Summary
`freshId` picks a free id by `stat`-ing candidates and returning the first miss; `createRun` then creates that directory. Nothing reserves the id between the two, so two concurrent creates take the same one and the second's manifest overwrites the first's.

## Description
lib/foundry/extract/store.ts:97-109 loops `stat(EXTRACT_ROOT/<id>)` and returns the first id that throws ENOENT; lib/foundry/extract/store.ts:121-149 then does `mkdir(..., { recursive: true })`, writes the sources, and writes run.json. Two calls with the same slug on the same day interleave between the stat and the mkdir and both get `2026-08-29-<slug>`: the sources land in one directory under colliding `sNN` names and the second `run.json` replaces the first, so one upload set is orphaned and one run silently describes the wrong images. The fix is to make the DIRECTORY the reservation — `mkdir` without `recursive` throws EEXIST atomically, so the loop becomes create-or-try-the-next-suffix and the id is held by the same syscall that proves it was free. That is the registry's guard-key-design shape: the key that names the operation is also what claims it.

## Flow
- two creates with the same slug land in the same second (a double-submit, or the CLI and the page)
- both stat, both see nothing, both take `2026-08-29-<slug>`
- both write sources/s01.jpg …, then both write run.json
- the surviving manifest lists the loser's file names with the winner's expectations

## Expected impact
One upload set is lost and the surviving run describes images that are not the ones it was given, with no error anywhere. Measured by racing two creates and counting distinct ids. What could break: the EEXIST loop must not mistake a permission error for a taken id.

## Evaluation
Claim: resilience — concurrent creates get distinct runs
Before: not taken — the instrument is missing. Racing two `createRun` calls requires a temp EXTRACT_ROOT, which the module does not allow (see the coverage finding).
After: not taken — see above
Method: probe — MISSING INSTRUMENT. The claim rests on reading the stat-then-mkdir gap; the race is real by construction and unmeasured here.
Result: unmeasurable
Gate: none
evidence:
lib/foundry/extract/store.ts:97-109 — freshId: stat-then-return, no reservation
lib/foundry/extract/store.ts:121-123 — mkdir(..., { recursive: true }), which succeeds on an existing directory
NOT MEASURED: it needs the disk-fixture harness the finding above describes, which is why this one is not built.

title: Both run listings read two files per run sequentially, next to a sibling that does not
body:
## Summary
`listRuns` and `listExtractRuns` await two JSON reads inside a `for` loop, so the page's boot call costs 2N round trips; `getCatalogue`, in the same file, reads its two files with `Promise.all`.

## Description
lib/foundry/store.ts:106-123 and lib/foundry/extract/store.ts:163-180 both loop over the run directory awaiting `readJson(run.json)` then `readJson(verdicts.json)` before moving to the next name. lib/foundry/store.ts:132-138 shows the convention the file already holds. The reads are independent — nothing in the loop depends on a previous run — so the whole listing is one `Promise.all` over the names. This is the registry's batching-and-n-plus-one shape at file-system scale.

## Flow
- the /foundry page loads
- GET /api/foundry/runs walks every run directory, two awaits at a time
- the page waits for 2N serialised reads where N is every run ever forged

## Expected impact
The first paint of the foundry page is bounded by run COUNT rather than by disk. What could break: an unbounded Promise.all over a very large directory opens many descriptors at once, so the batch wants a concurrency cap.

## Evaluation
Claim: performance — the run listing stops being serialised in the run count
Before: not taken — foundry-out/ is absent on this machine, so N is 0 and the path cannot be timed. The instrument missing is a populated runs directory (or the temp-root seam above).
After: not taken — see above; the change is 2N sequential reads to ceil(2N/limit) batched ones
Method: probe — read both loops against the sibling that already batches; measurement blocked on having runs on disk
Result: unmeasurable
Gate: none
evidence:
lib/foundry/store.ts:106-123 — sequential awaits in the loop
lib/foundry/extract/store.ts:163-180 — the same
lib/foundry/store.ts:132-138 — getCatalogue, Promise.all, same file

title: An off-vocabulary readback is now scored honestly but still nowhere recorded
body:
## Summary
`isReadback` accepts any string for an observable while `validateSynthesis` refuses anything outside `ENUMS`, so a drifted vision word is stored on the manifest and — since 893fe0b — quietly dropped from the score, with nothing in the run log saying a field went unread.

## Description
lib/foundry/extract/engine.ts's `isReadback` checks `typeof o[f] === "string"` and nothing more; lib/foundry/extract/vocabulary.ts's `validateSynthesis` checks `ENUMS[f].includes(v)` and refuses the whole synthesis otherwise. The scoring half of that asymmetry was closed this round — an off-vocabulary word is unmeasured rather than a miss — but the OBSERVABILITY half is open: the value is written into `source.readback` as if it were vocabulary, the field simply vanishes from `per_field`, and `ExtractBoard` renders one chip fewer with no indication that anything was skipped. The forge's own `Grade` type, one module over, carries `unmeasured: string[]` with the note "Non-empty means the grade is partial" — the repo already has the vocabulary for this and the extract side does not use it. Fixed means the run log naming the field and the value it got, so a vendor drifting its vocabulary is visible as a cause rather than as a slightly different number. Adding `unmeasured` to `Scored` would change a persisted manifest shape, which is why it is not a one-line change.

## Flow
- a vision model answers "semi-realistic" for surface_realism
- the readback is stored, the field is dropped from the score, the chip row shows 7 instead of 8
- nobody can tell from the run whether the model drifted or the field simply agreed

## Expected impact
The extraction pipeline's own quality signal degrades invisibly — the registry's extraction-observability technique names exactly this ("failure rate steady while output quality decays"). Measured by whether a drifted field appears in the run log. What could break: adding a field to `Scored` changes what is written into every manifest, so the reader has to tolerate its absence on older runs.

## Evaluation
Claim: quality — a vendor's vocabulary drift becomes visible as a cause instead of a smaller number
Before: 0 of 8 observable fields report when they were unreadable; the run log records nothing about vocabulary drift
After: a drifted field is named in the run log with the value it returned
Method: probe — read the two validators against each other and traced where a dropped field surfaces (it does not)
Result: better
Gate: none
evidence:
lib/foundry/extract/engine.ts — isReadback: `typeof o[f] === "string"`, no enum check
lib/foundry/extract/vocabulary.ts — validateSynthesis: `ENUMS[f].includes(v)` or refuse
lib/foundry/types.ts:29-30 — the forge's Grade.unmeasured, with the principle already written down
app/foundry/ExtractBoard.tsx:249 — Object.entries(perField), so a dropped field is simply one chip fewer

title: The Python half of this repo has no automated verification of any kind

## Summary
Four scripts that spend hours of GPU and write the repo's versioned indices are covered by no typecheck, no linter and no test lane — every gate this repo owns is TypeScript-shaped.

## Description
`.github/workflows/gates.yml` runs nine blocking steps and not one of them reads a `.py` file: `tsc --noEmit` sees only the TS project, `eslint.config.mjs` matches no Python, and the probe lane is `@playwright/test` over TS modules. `.ai/manifest.yaml` declares no Python capability. So `pipeline/foundry/*.py` — which owns the WRITE side of ledger.json and styles.json, the two files lib/foundry/store.ts calls "the finding" — is verified by nothing at all. All three defects fixed in this round were found by reading and confirmed by probes written for the occasion; none of them could have been caught by anything standing. ## Flow

- typecheck, lint, probes, build and bundle all pass, because none of them look
- the defect surfaces on the next evening-long run, or does not surface at all

## Expected impact
The only part of the repo where a bug costs hours of GPU is the only part with no gate. Measured by counting blocking steps that read a .py file. What could break: a Python step needs an interpreter in CI, and a check that cannot run must be could-not-run rather than green — the lint ratchet's three-exit-code shape is the model.

title: A resumed run loses the prompt and workflow of every candidate it resumes
body:
## Summary
`stage_generate` treats a PNG on disk as a finished generation — correct for the image, but it then skips the block that writes the sidecar, so the candidates that survived a crash are the ones with no record of how they were made.

## Description
pipeline/foundry/forge.py: the resume path marks `c["status"] = "generated"` from `(run_dir / c["file"]).exists()` and drops the candidate out of `todo`. Everything the generation branch writes afterwards — `c["prompt"]`, `c["timings"]`, and the `<candidate>.json` sidecar carrying the prompt AND the full Flux workflow — is therefore never written for it. The manifest's own header advertises that sidecar as part of a run (`scenes/<scene>/candidates/<...>.json   prompt + workflow + grade`), lib/foundry/types.ts declares `sidecar` as a required field on every Candidate, and `commitRun` unlinks it on reject. So a resumed run produces candidates the cull can grade and a human can keep, whose provenance — which recipe, which window, which seed produced this plate — exists only in the PNG. `--resume` is a documented first-class flag in the module docstring; this is the path taken after every crash, which is exactly when provenance matters most. Fixed means writing the sidecar from the manifest on the resume path, or recording that the candidate was adopted rather than generated.

## Flow
- a run dies mid-generate (a recycle that would not take, a killed process)
- `--resume` adopts every PNG already on disk as generated
- those candidates never get a sidecar, and never get `prompt` on the manifest
- the cull shows them beside fully-recorded ones with no visible difference

## Expected impact
The forge's whole output is a judgement about which recipe works; a kept candidate that cannot say which recipe made it is evidence with the label torn off. Measured by resuming a run and counting candidates with a file but no sidecar. What could break: writing a sidecar after the fact must not claim a `generate_s` timing nobody measured.

## Evaluation
Claim: quality — a resumed candidate keeps the record of how it was made
Before: not taken — the instrument is a real run with candidates on disk, which needs the rig. By reading: every candidate adopted on resume has 0 sidecars and no `prompt` field.
After: not taken — every adopted candidate carries the same sidecar a generated one does
Method: probe — MISSING INSTRUMENT (a run directory with plates). The path is unambiguous in the source; the count is not takeable here.
Result: unmeasurable
Gate: none
evidence:
pipeline/foundry/forge.py stage_generate — the resume block sets status from the PNG and removes the candidate from `todo`
same function — `c["prompt"]`, `c["timings"]` and the sidecar write all live in the generation branch below
pipeline/foundry/forge.py module docstring — the sidecar is advertised as part of a run
lib/foundry/types.ts — `sidecar: string` is required on Candidate
NOT MEASURED: needs a run with plates on disk, which needs the GPU rig; the code path is unambiguous by reading.

title: A run whose generation aborted still reports `done`
body:
## Summary
When ComfyUI cannot be recycled after a failure, `stage_generate` breaks out of its loop and leaves the remaining candidates `pending` — and `main()` then sets the manifest to `done`.

## Description
pipeline/foundry/forge.py: the generation loop's failure branch ends `if not guard.recycle_comfy("after failure"): break`. That break is right — the engine is gone and every further candidate would fail the same way — but nothing above it records that the stage was abandoned. Control returns to `main()`, which grades whatever was generated and unconditionally writes `status = "done"`, `finished`, and a progress block. The page reads that status, and `commitRun` in lib/foundry/store.ts gates on exactly it (`if (!["done","failed"].includes(run.status))`), so an aborted run is committable and its untouched candidates are silently outside the cull. The printed summary does say `N/M candidates graded`, so the number is honest while the status is not. Fixed is a status that distinguishes a run that finished from a run that stopped — the manifest already has `failed`, and `partial` would be more honest than either.

## Flow
- the card is lost mid-generate and the recycle will not take
- the loop breaks with candidates still pending
- grading runs over what exists, and the manifest says `done`
- /foundry offers Commit on a run that generated half its grid

## Expected impact
The status is the one field every consumer routes on, and it says the opposite of what happened. Measured by killing ComfyUI mid-run and reading the status. What could break: a new status value is a shape change the TS `RunStatus` union has to learn, which makes this a contract-adjacent edit rather than a one-liner.

## Evaluation
Claim: resilience — a run that stopped does not report that it finished
Before: not taken — needs the rig to abort a real run. By reading: the break leaves N candidates `pending` and the status written is `done` regardless of N.
After: not taken — the status distinguishes finished from stopped
Method: probe — MISSING INSTRUMENT (a live ComfyUI to kill). Unambiguous by reading; the fix touches the shared RunStatus union, which is why it is not a one-liner.
Result: unmeasurable
Gate: contract
evidence:
pipeline/foundry/forge.py stage_generate — `if not guard.recycle_comfy("after failure"): break`
pipeline/foundry/forge.py main() — `manifest["status"] = "done"` with no check on what the stage left behind
lib/foundry/types.ts — `RunStatus` union; commitRun gates on done|failed

title: The reader in lib/foundry closes the last 7% of the torn-catalogue window, and turns it into a 500
body:
## Summary
With the write side fixed (2aa053d) the residue is a PermissionError the READER gets during the rename — and `readJson` rethrows anything that is not ENOENT, into a route with no catch.

## Description
Measured this round: after the atomic write with retry, a reader polling the 30 KB catalogue in a tight loop still saw 43-65 PermissionErrors per 40 writes (~4-7% of reads), and ZERO FileNotFoundError. That last fact is the good news — `readJson(STYLES, {styles: []})` in lib/foundry/store.ts catches only ENOENT, so the window can never present an EMPTY catalogue as fact. It presents a throw instead, and `app/api/foundry/styles/route.ts` is the one foundry route with no `try/catch`, so it surfaces as an unhandled 500 on the page's boot call. Fixed is a short retry on the read, the mirror of the one now on the write — and it also revives a finding this sweep REJECTED in round 2 as not-better, on the reasoning that `getCatalogue` could not raise a FoundryError. That reasoning was right and the conclusion was wrong: the risk was never FoundryError, it is a transient OS error from a concurrent writer, and round 3 measured it.

## Flow
- the operator runs `acquire.py`, or the CLI extract commits a style
- the page's catalogue poll lands inside the rename
- readFile raises EPERM, readJson rethrows, the route has no catch
- /foundry answers 500 on the call that loads the whole styles surface

## Expected impact
A 4-7% failure rate on the page's boot call for the duration of any catalogue write. Measured by counting unusable reads per write, which is the same probe this round already used. What could break: a read retry must not mask a genuinely unreadable file — bound the attempts and let the last one throw.

## Evaluation
Claim: resilience — the catalogue read survives a concurrent catalogue write
Before: 4-7% of reads unusable during a write (43-65 PermissionError per 40 writes), each one an unhandled 500
After: 0 unusable, with a bounded retry that still throws on a genuinely unreadable file
Method: probe — drove the real writer against a polling reader at the real file size, three runs
Result: better
Gate: none
evidence:
measured 2026-08-29, real 30 KB catalogue, reader in a tight loop, 40 writes:
  after the write fix: torn 0 | PermissionError 43-65 | FileNotFoundError 0
lib/foundry/store.ts readJson — `if (code === "ENOENT") return fallback; throw e;`
app/api/foundry/styles/route.ts — the only foundry route with no try/catch

## Summary
CullGrid, FoundryView and ExtractBoard contain zero `aria-`, `role=`, `tabIndex` and `useAnnounce` between them. Tiles are `<div onClick>`, the focus ring is app state the browser knows nothing about, and no verdict is ever announced.

## Description

Nothing in the grid takes browser focus — `Tile` renders a div with `onClick` and no `tabIndex` — so an assistive user tabbing the page never reaches a candidate, is never told one is selected, and hears nothing when K records a keep. `scrollIntoView` moves the viewport and not the caret. The app HAS the channel for this: lib/announcer.tsx is mounted at the root and app/library/AssetsBrowser.tsx already announces `asset-removed`. ## Flow

- Tab walks the tab strip, the run list and the row K/X buttons, and never enters the grid
- arrows move a cursor that is announced nowhere; K records a verdict silently

After: grid semantics on the grid, the cursor IS browser focus, one announcement per verdict

title: Verdict saves have no ordering guard, so a cleared verdict can come back
body:
## Summary
The read path got a monotonic ticket in 7aef3aa; the write path did not. Two debounced whole-map PUTs can land out of order, and because `U` CLEARS a verdict a later map is not always a superset of an earlier one.

## Description
`setVerdict` in app/foundry/FoundryView.tsx (and its twin in ExtractView.tsx) debounces 400ms and then PUTs the ENTIRE verdict map. Two saves are in flight whenever the user pauses more than 400ms twice in quick succession while the first request is still open. The server's `putVerdicts` is a whole-map replace with no version or ticket, so whichever request the handler processes last wins. For a pure keep/reject stream that is harmless — every later map contains every earlier decision. It stops being harmless for `U`, which deletes a key: if the map that RESTORES a verdict is processed after the map that cleared it, the clear is undone, and the user's last action is the one that vanished. The read side already carries the fix and the reasoning (`detailTicket`, "arrival order is not issue order"); the write side is the same sentence unwritten. Fixed is the same monotonic ticket around the save, or a version the server refuses to go backwards from.

## Flow
- press K on a candidate, pause; the 400ms save fires
- press U on the same candidate before that request returns; a second save fires
- the second request is handled first, the first is handled second
- the candidate is keep again, and nothing on the page disagrees

## Expected impact
A deliberate correction silently reverts, on the surface whose entire output is the human's judgement. Measured by issuing two overlapping PUTs in a known order and reading the stored map. What could break: a ticket on the client cannot stop a server that processed them out of order, so the honest fix may need the version on the request.

## Evaluation
Claim: resilience — the last verdict a human pressed is the one that is stored
Before: not taken — needs controlled request reordering. By reading: 1 of 2 paths carries an ordering guard; `U` makes a later map a strict subset, so the loss is possible in principle.
After: not taken — both paths guarded
Method: probe — MISSING INSTRUMENT (a way to reorder two in-flight PUTs). The asymmetry with the read path is unambiguous in the source.
Result: unmeasurable
Gate: none
evidence:
app/foundry/FoundryView.tsx setVerdict — 400ms debounce, then saveVerdicts(runId, next) with no ticket
app/foundry/ExtractView.tsx — the same shape
lib/foundry/store.ts putVerdicts — whole-map replace, no version
app/foundry/FoundryView.tsx detailTicket — the fix, on the READ path, with the reasoning already written out
NOT MEASURED: needs two overlapping requests with controlled arrival order; the local server makes reordering rare but nothing prevents it.

title: The 4s poll starts a new request whether or not the last one came back
body:
## Summary
`usePolling` fires on a fixed interval with no in-flight check, so a slow or hung `/api/foundry/runs/<id>` accumulates concurrent requests against the rate limiter that lib/apiAuth.ts sizes for exactly this traffic.

## Description
lib/usePolling.ts calls `fnRef.current()` every `ms` unconditionally. FoundryView's poll issues TWO requests per tick (`loadDetail` + `loadRuns`), so a run manifest that takes longer than four seconds to serialise — a large sweep rewrites run.json after every candidate — has three or four sets in flight before the first returns. Correctness is protected by the detail ticket, so no stale data lands; what is spent is requests. lib/apiAuth.ts names "a 4-second poll of a live run plus a debounced verdict autosave" as the shape its bucket is sized against, and this doubles or triples that under exactly the condition (a big live run) where the poll matters. usePolling was written this morning to stop polling a HIDDEN tab; this is the other half of the same economy. Fixed is a skip-if-in-flight flag, which the hook can own for every caller rather than each surface inventing it.

## Flow
- a large run is live and its manifest is slow to serve
- the interval fires again before the previous pair returned
- requests stack for as long as the run stays slow
- the limiter counts every one of them

## Expected impact
Wasted requests against a bucket the repo deliberately sized, at the moment the surface is under most load. Measured by counting requests issued per interval under a delayed response. What could break: skipping a tick when one is in flight must not skip forever if a request never settles — it needs a timeout or a generation counter.

## Evaluation
Claim: performance — a slow response stops multiplying requests
Before: not taken — no run on disk to poll here. By reading: 2 requests per tick, unconditionally, with no in-flight check anywhere in the chain.
After: not taken — at most one set in flight per surface
Method: probe — MISSING INSTRUMENT (a live run and a delayed response). The absence of any in-flight guard is unambiguous.
Result: unmeasurable
Gate: none

## Summary
Two unhandled rejections sat on the app's most-polled surface until they were read by eye, and no gate could have found them — the linter has no rule for it and the probe lane cannot observe one.

## Description
The defect fixed in 6ffecfb is a `.then(fn)` with no rejection path. `eslint.config.mjs` runs `eslint-config-next` plus a short list of hand-chosen rules; none of them is `@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises` or `promise/catch-or-return`, and the first needs typed linting (`parserOptions.projectService`), which this config does not enable. So the whole class is invisible: the two found this round were on a 4s poll, in the two largest components of a context, and the tree was green throughout. Fixed is typed linting plus the rule, ratcheted like the react-hooks buckets already are — the population will not be zero on first run, and lint-baseline.json is exactly the instrument for that. This is an app-infrastructure change (eslint.config.mjs), not this context's, which is why it is filed rather than done.

## Flow
- a promise is started with no rejection path
- typecheck, lint, probes, build and bundle all pass
- in this app GlobalErrorBridge then narrates the failure as a storage write, assertively

## Expected impact
The class is not cosmetic here: an unhandled rejection is routed to the user as a WRONG message, so every one of them is a UX defect and not just a missing log. Measured by whether a seeded floating promise reddens the gate. What could break: typed linting is materially slower and the first run will surface a population that has to be baselined in the same commit.

## Summary
`lib/text/router.ts` is what .ai/manifest.yaml names as `engines.text.chokepoint`, it walks a documented fallback ladder, and no probe in the 38-file lane imports it.

## Description
The manifest declares the ladder — local CLI, then a metered Gemini key, then honest refusal — and records that one rung was unverified until `npm run verify:text -- --spend` drove real turns through it. That command is deliberately NOT in `npm test` because it talks to a vendor, which is correct. But the LADDER ITSELF is pure: which rung is chosen for a posture, when it descends, what `reroutedFrom` records, and what the bottom does when nothing is available. All of that is decidable without a vendor, and `style-extract.probe.spec.ts` already shows the shape — it drives the extract engine's whole state machine through an IO fake and runs for free. The gap is not theoretical: the transport defect fixed this session in `f59c27a` (an unhandled stdin error taking the server down instead of letting the ladder descend) lived on the ladder's first rung, and nothing in the lane could have caught it. Fixed is a probe that drives `reason()` against a fake provider set, asserting the descent order, the refusal, and the provenance each rung stamps.

## Flow
- a change lands in lib/text/
- 320 probes pass, because none of them import it
- the ladder is exercised only by a command that costs money and is not in the gate
- the first real evidence is a route failing in front of a user

## Expected impact
The one seam the manifest calls a chokepoint, unguarded by the lane built to guard seams. Measured by whether any probe imports it. What could break: a fake provider set has to stay honest about what a real one does — the dated `enforcesSchema` flag is exactly the kind of thing a fake quietly gets wrong.

body:
## Summary
`PROVIDERS` is a module-private const in lib/text/router.ts, so the new probe can drive the plan, the steer rules and the refusal — but never a turn that succeeds, and therefore never the rung labelling, `reroutedFrom` or the schemaEnforcement downgrade.

## Description
lib/foundry/extract/engine.ts takes its whole world through an `EngineIO` parameter, which is why its state machine is covered by 11 probes driving 73 assertions against fakes. The text router constructs its providers from a private table instead, so the only way to reach a successful serve is to call a vendor. The consequence is precise and it is the interesting half of the ladder: the properties the header calls the two that make it a ladder rather than a pile — "selection is inspectable" (`provenance.rung` and `transport` travel with every answer) and "descent has a reason" (`reroutedFrom` carries the trail into staged output that outlives the process) — are the two nothing can currently assert. Fixed is an injection point of the same shape the sibling module already uses: an optional providers argument defaulting to the real table, used by `reason` and `engineStatus`. That is a production change to enable testing, which the registry's repo-testing technique treats as a legitimate design decision rather than a smell — and this repo has already made it once, next door.

## Flow
- a change alters how the rung is labelled, or drops `reroutedFrom` from the provenance
- 337 probes pass, because none of them can reach a successful serve
- the receipt on a staged plan silently stops saying which engine wrote it

## Expected impact
The ladder's inspectability is its stated reason for existing and it is the part with no test. Measured by whether a probe can assert a rung label without a vendor. What could break: an injectable provider table is a new way for production code to be handed the wrong providers, so the default must stay the real table and the parameter must be test-only in practice.

## Evaluation
Claim: quality — the ladder's two stated properties become assertable without a vendor
Before: 0 of the ladder's success-path properties (rung, reroutedFrom, schemaEnforcement) can be asserted; 10 cases now cover the plan, steer and refusal paths
After: all three assertable against fakes, through an optional providers argument
Method: probe — wrote the vendor-free probe and found the exact boundary it could not cross
Result: better
Gate: none

title: The engine's availability oracle asks one question the router does not
body:
## Summary
`engineStatus` calls `provider.probe()` for every unblocked candidate; `reason`'s walk deliberately probes only keyless providers. Its docstring says it "cannot report an availability the router disagrees with".

## Description
In `walk()` the expensive gate is guarded — `if (!KEY_VAR[id]) { const p = await provider.probe(); ... }` — with the reasoning attached: a key-holding provider's 401 arrives fast and is classified `no-key`, so paying for a probe would be the wrong trade. `engineStatus` has no such guard. Today the divergence is harmless because google's `probe()` is a key-presence check that re-asks exactly what `cheapBlock` just asked, so the answers agree and the cost is one redundant call. It stops being harmless the moment any key-holding adapter's probe does something a config lookup cannot settle — which is precisely what a probe is FOR, and what the registry's availability-probe technique describes. At that point the diagnostics surface and the router would disagree about who can serve, and the docstring would still say they cannot. Fixed is either the same `if (!KEY_VAR[id])` guard, or a docstring that says it probes MORE than the router does and why.

## Flow
- a key-holding adapter grows a probe that actually reaches the vendor
- engineStatus starts spending, or reporting a provider down that the router would use
- the docstring still says the two cannot disagree

## Expected impact
A diagnostics surface that is trusted precisely because it claims to mirror the router. Measured by comparing the two gates' code paths. What could break: adding the guard means engineStatus reports a key-holding provider as ok on key presence alone, which is what the router already assumes — so the honest fix may be the docstring rather than the guard.

## Evaluation
Claim: quality — the oracle's claim about itself is true, or stops being made
Before: 2 gates in the router's walk, 2 gates in engineStatus, but one of them asks a different question for key-holding providers; 0 disagreements today because google's probe is free
After: either the same guard, or a docstring that names the difference
Method: probe — traced both gate paths and read google's probe to establish that the divergence is currently harmless
Result: better
Gate: none
evidence:
lib/text/router.ts walk() — `if (!KEY_VAR[id])` before `await provider.probe()`
lib/text/router.ts engineStatus() — `const p = await PROVIDERS[id]().probe()`, unguarded
lib/text/router.ts engineStatus docstring — "asks the same two gates, so it cannot report an availability the router disagrees with"
lib/text/providers/google.ts probe() — a key-presence check, free today, which is why nothing diverges yet

title: judgeProof can still void the basis of a lock, and only a view stops it
body:
## Summary
The ratchet guard added in 8c1467e sits on `update`. `judgeProof` is a separate write path with no guard, so flipping a locked theme's only approval to rejected leaves it `locked` with zero approvals — a state `canLock` would refuse to create.

## Description
`useThemes.judgeProof(id, proofId, state)` commits a new proofs array directly; nothing asks whether the theme is locked. Flip the last `approved` proof to `rejected` on a locked sheet and `statusOf` still says locked (it reads `lockedAt`), while `canLock` on the same record is now false and `lockBlocker` would say "every proof was rejected — generate another". That is the lock gate's own refusal condition, reached from the other side, on a record that is already anchoring projects. What prevents it today is app/library/parts.tsx passing `onJudge={locked ? undefined : ...}` — the same shape of protection the update path had before this round, in a different component. Fixed is the same treatment: extend `ratchetBlocker` (or a sibling) to cover a proofs patch that would remove the last approval from a locked theme, and have `judgeProof` ask it. Note the deliberate asymmetry it must preserve: ADDING a proof to a locked sheet stays allowed, so the rule is about approvals going away, not about the sheet being immutable.

## Flow
- a locked style anchors two projects
- someone reopens its sheet and rejects the one approved proof
- statusOf still says locked, so every consumer still treats it as ratified
- the evidence the lock was granted on no longer exists

## Expected impact
A lock that outlives its evidence, on the record every project's look is bound to. Measured by constructing that patch and asking the guard. What could break: the rule must not freeze the sheet — promoting a plate onto a locked style is a deliberate, documented allowance and would be easy to break while closing this.

## Evaluation
Claim: quality — a lock cannot outlive the approvals it was granted on
Before: 1 of 2 mutating write paths asks the ratchet; the other is guarded by one prop in one component
After: 2 of 2, with adding a proof to a locked sheet still allowed
Method: probe — read judgeProof against canLock and statusOf, and found the view that is currently holding the rule
Result: better
Gate: none
evidence:
lib/useThemes.ts judgeProof — commits a new proofs array with no lock check
lib/themes.ts canLock — `approvedProofs(t).length > 0 && every(p => p.state !== "pending")`
lib/themes.ts statusOf — reads lockedAt only, so the record still reports locked
app/library/parts.tsx — `onJudge={locked ? undefined : ...}`, the view-held guard
commit 8c1467e — the same class, closed on the update path

title: Both spend ceilings check without reserving, so concurrent calls can walk straight through them
body:
## Summary
`assertWithinMusicBudget` reads recorded spend, compares, and returns; the debit happens after the vendor call. Two calls that overlap both see the same pre-spend figure and both pass — and the window between the check and the debit is the ENTIRE vendor call, which for audio is seconds to minutes.

## Description
lib/music/budget.ts: `assertWithinMusicBudget(pending)` computes `currentMusicSeconds()` (recorded rows only) and throws if `spent + pending > ceiling`. `lib/music/elevenlabs.ts`'s `metered()` then calls the vendor and only afterwards calls `recordMusicSpend`. Nothing reserves the pending amount in between, and nothing serialises the two. With a 300s ceiling, 200s spent and two overlapping 80s cues, both read 200, both compute 280, both pass, and 360s lands — a 20% overrun of a control whose entire job is to bound spend. A music call may ask for up to 600s, so the overrun scales with the call. lib/imaging/budget.ts has the identical shape in USD, which makes this one design decision across both money ceilings rather than a drift between them. BOTH headers name the SCALE-OUT limitation — "good enough for a single-instance prototype", "in-memory, per-process" — and neither names this one, which bites on a single instance. Fixed is a reservation: record the pending amount before the call and reconcile it after (to the actual on success, removed on a refusal that was not billed), which is the same shape `BILLED_ON_FAILURE` already reasons about on the other side of the call.

## Flow
- two cue renders are started close together (two tabs, a batch audition, two extract runs stepping)
- both call the ceiling check before either has returned from the vendor
- both see the same recorded spend and both pass
- both are billed, and the ceiling reports the overrun only afterwards

## Expected impact
A spend ceiling that can be exceeded by the number of calls in flight, on the two paths in the app that cost real money. Measured by issuing two overlapping calls against a ceiling that admits only one and counting what is recorded. What could break: a reservation must be released on every exit path or a crashed call strangles the window until it rolls over — which is the failure mode that makes naive reservations worse than none.

## Evaluation
Claim: quality — the ceiling bounds spend rather than bounding it per caller
Before: overrun window = the duration of one vendor call (seconds to minutes for audio); 2 concurrent 80s cues against a 300s ceiling with 200s spent record 360s
After: 0 overrun: the second caller sees the first's reservation and is refused before the vendor is called
Method: probe — traced check-to-debit through metered() in both engines and confirmed no lock, no reservation, and no mention of the window in either header
Result: better
Gate: none
evidence:
lib/music/budget.ts assertWithinMusicBudget — reads currentMusicSeconds(), compares, returns; no reservation
lib/music/elevenlabs.ts metered() — assert, then await the vendor, then recordMusicSpend
lib/imaging/budget.ts assertWithinBudget — identical shape in USD
lib/imaging/budget.ts:22 and lib/music/budget.ts:38 — both name the per-process/scale-out limit; neither names the check-to-debit window
SPANS TWO CONTEXTS (music-pipeline and imaging-providers): fixing one and not the other would recreate exactly the drift this sweep keeps finding, so it is filed whole rather than half-built (veto 1).

title: The music provenance record holds two of the five facts the standard names
body:
## Summary
`MusicProvenance` is `{vendor, modelId, requestedMs, plan, generatedAt}`. The rights-and-provenance-record technique names five things a record must hold at generation time; three are absent, including the one it calls load-bearing.

## Description
Against the technique item by item: **vendor/model/date** — present. **The brief** — present, and generously so: the whole `MusicPlan` is kept, which is both the reproducibility anchor and the evidence of human creative input the technique asks for. **Account and plan tier at generation time** — ABSENT, and this is the one the technique calls load-bearing, because vendor commercial grants are plan-scoped and NON-RETROACTIVE: upgrading later licenses nothing generated earlier. **Reference material used and its status** — ABSENT, and not vacuously: lib/music/elevenlabs.ts explicitly supports audio-reference chunks and `source_composition_plan` for section edits, so the app really can anchor a render on other audio and keeps no record that it did. A reference's rights exposure propagates into the output. **Intended destination cleared for** — ABSENT; clearance is per-destination and a track re-purposed later gets re-cleared against the record. The technique's own framing is why this is worth filing rather than shrugging at: these facts "exist fully at generation time, decay from the moment the take is accepted, and are routinely unreconstructable by delivery". Fixed is deciding what this product records — which is a product and legal call, not a refactor, and it changes a record that travels with a track.

## Flow
- a creator renders cues over months, on whatever plan they were on that week
- one video is later used commercially
- nothing on any track says which account, which tier, or whether a reference was anchored
- the facts needed to clear it existed only at generation time

## Expected impact
Whether generated music may be used commercially is a property of the circumstances, and the circumstances are not being kept. Measured by holding the record against the technique's five items. What could break: adding fields to a record that travels with a track is a persisted-format change, and the tier cannot be read without asking the vendor or the operator — which is exactly why this is a decision rather than an edit.

## Evaluation
Claim: quality — a track can be cleared from its own record rather than from memory
Before: 2 of the 5 facts the standard names are recorded; the load-bearing one and the reference status are not
After: 5 of 5, or a stated decision about which this product does not keep and why
Method: probe — compared MusicProvenance field by field against the technique, and checked the reference path is real rather than hypothetical
Result: unmeasurable
Gate: contract

## Summary
The notebook flags a claim as load-bearing at low confidence, the app counts it and renders the count in red, and `suggestedReason` already writes the sentence explaining it needs a second source - but nothing queues a deepen for it. The creator has to notice it and click.

## Description
